entry.dc:title: The effects of surface mining of coal on water quality near Grande Cache, Alberta.
entry.dc:creator: Hackbarth D.
entry.dc:description: The effects of mining activity on water quality vary in intensity but follow a consistent pattern. The relative proportion of the various cations does not change; however, their concentrations may rise to four times background values. The concentration of anions also increases and there is a shift in the relative proportions from bicarbonate to sulfate and, at the more strongly affected sites, to nitrate. The distribution of pH values is not significantly different from unaffected sites. -from Author

entry.dc:title: Toxic substances from coal energy: An overview
entry.dc:creator: Shy C.M.
entry.dc:description: Environmental concerns over increased coal consumption are fully justified by the past history of coal use. Although improved technology has provided some safeguards, increased utilization will require mining practices, emission control technologies, and waste disposal procedures that are not yet fully integrated into the routine use of the coal energy system. The Committee on Health and Environmental Effects of Increased Coal Utilization identified six critical environmental issues which are of concern: coal mine worker health and safety, reclamation of arid lands from surface mining, the health effects of coal combustion products, toxic trace elements in coal combustion wastes, acid fallout, and global effects of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. This presentation addresses the first four of these issues.

entry.dc:title: Planning erosion control for coal mining and reclamaton ( Iowa, USA).
entry.dc:creator: Anderson C.
entry.dc:description: The special problems relating to surface mining and erosion are briefly described and methods of control on active and reclaimed mines are noted. Describes the Iowa Coal Project mine experiment in which a series of bench terraces, parallel to the original contour were used to fit the post-mining land use and to minimise likely erosion. Measures taken to ensure adequate drainage and to preserve the overburden during the slip mining operation are described.-R.H.Johnson

entry.dc:title: The hydrogeology of the Athabasca Oil Sands area, Alberta.
entry.dc:creator: Hackbarth D.
entry.dc:description: West of a major fault 3 hydrostratigraphic units are defined. Two hydrostratigraphic units merge E of the fault. Groundwater flows W towards the fault, with total dissolved solids concentrations seldom exceeding 50 000mg/L. On a regional basis, the oil sands have a finite hydraulic conductivity commonly of 10<sup>-6</sup> to 10<sup>-4</sup>cm/sec. Surface mining ventures will generally require that the oil sands and underlying aquifers be depressurized. Structural conditions are suitable for injection of waste liquids into the D- 2 hydrostratigraphic unit only west of the limits of evaporite solution. -after Authors

entry.dc:title: Surface mining reclamation in Appalachia: impact of the 1977 Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act ( USA).
entry.dc:creator: Sweeney L.
entry.dc:description: Reclamation procedures used in Appalachian hill areas have often created level bench or plateau landforms and soils which are of greater value than were the original hillslopes and soils. In West Virginia considerable success in reclamation of mined areas has been achieved by the use of a coal tax, but the rest of the U.S.A. so far has not employed this means of financing redevelopment measures.-R.H.Johnson

entry.dc:title: Lignite Mining in the Rhine Basin.
entry.dc:creator: Bastidon J.
entry.dc:description: In 1977, West German lignite production rose to 123 million tons, of which 88% came from the Rhine Basin. This article describes the mining methods employed in the basin, and then analyzes mining and other costs of the Rhine lignite. Surface mining and land reclamation are also discussed.

entry.dc:title: KEEP YOUR BLASTING UNDER CONTROL.
entry.dc:creator: Dick R.
entry.dc:description: To protect various structures from the adverse effect of overburden blasting, the Office of Surface Mining (OSM) gives the mine operator three possible alternatives. This article discusses the three options, and explains how to choose among them in order to comply with the new regulations. Control of blast vibrations is also discussed.

entry.dc:title: DRAGLINES CAN REDUCE SURFACE MINING COSTS.
entry.dc:creator: Morey P.
entry.dc:description: Draglines are often the most effective way to surface mine coal. This article briefly explains how to develop dragline stripping mine designs that use the dragline in the most efficient and economic way. Dragline production simulation is also considered.

entry.dc:title: RIP INSTEAD OF DRILLING AND BLASTING.
entry.dc:creator: Jackson D.
entry.dc:description: As tractor size, weight and horsepower have steadily increased, the use of rippers has expanded dramatically in surface mining, both in their capabilities and applications. Harder materials can be ripped to greater depths at higher production rates than ever before, offering economic advantages over drilling and blasting. One company, CRC Kelley, now offers a 179-in. -long ripper shank to match the strength of the new super dozers, a major leap in ripper capability. Units are now in operation in North Dakota and Colorado. Advantages of this tractor ripper are discussed, and its operating performance is evaluated.

entry.dc:title: SURFACE MINING AND THE HYDROLOGIC BALANCE.
entry.dc:creator: Curtis W.
entry.dc:description: A properly reclaimed mined watershed may have higher retention storage capacity than before mining. With proper surface treatment and vegetative cover, infiltration rates can be as high as or higher than before mining. Surface storage can be built in during the mining and reclamation phases. Surface impoundments can be strategically placed to control runoff and water movement. However, water quality may suffer after surface mining. More geologic materials are exposed to weathering, which can result in mineral or acid pollution in the streams. Care in moving and placing the overburden can minimize chemical release.

entry.dc:title: NEW LAND USES CREATED BY SURFACE MINING.
entry.dc:creator: Christy P.
entry.dc:description: Mined lands in Illinois are being restored to near their original use capabilities and in some cases to a more productive level than existed prior to mining. A brief description of the major types of surface mining equipment utilized and an elementary explanation of their fundamental operation aid in reviewing the tables and data are presented.

entry.dc:title: U. K. OPENCAST COAL MINING.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Although underground mining continues to account for most of the coal produced in the United Kingdom (during 1977 104. 5 million tonnes were produced from 231 collieries), the Opencast Executive of the U. K. National Coal Board (NCB) continues to expand its production capacity. In the U. K. , these surface mining operations are carried out on large opencast sites worked by contractors. This brief article looks at some of the sites operated by George Wimpey & Co. and considers the type of equipment used by this contractor.

entry.dc:title: CHALLENGES OF REVEGETATION.
entry.dc:creator: Alder G.M.
entry.dc:description: Proposed draft regulations from the Office of Surface Mining will require mine operators to revegetate surface mined lands to provide a plant cover that is ″diverse, effective, and permanent″ . The article defines the biological processes that underlie the terms.

entry.dc:title: Multiple objectives under uncertainty: An illustrative application of protrade
entry.dc:creator: Goicoechea A.
entry.dc:description: A decision making method labeled Protrade has been developed to account for both multiple objectives and uncertainty aspects. This method is applied to the case study of the Black Mesa Region in Northern Arizona which is being strip mined for coal. One important concern in large‐scale surface mining is the reclamation of mine spoils to bring about beneficial land uses while observing economic, social, environmental, and legal constraints. Protrade considers a set of linear objective functions with random parameters, subject to a set of physical constraints; the preferences of the decision maker are articulated in a progressive manner, and alternative solutions are generated. Nonlinear deterministic equivalents are introduced to account for uncertainty in some of the parameters involved. While no final policy recommendations are made, this illustration of Protrade is carried out to investigate the potential of the method for trading off multiple objectives and measures of uncertainty in water and other natural resource system design problems. Copyright 1979 by the American Geophysical Union.

entry.dc:title: SIMULATION OF THE EFFECTS OF SURFACE MINING ON GROUNDWATER IN THE POWDER RIVER BASIN.
entry.dc:creator: McIntosh G.
entry.dc:description: This paper discusses a US Bureau of Mines projects designed to assess and predict the impacts which surface project mining will have on the regional shallow groundwater systems in the Powder River Basin of Wyoming and Montana. The primary objective will be met through the accomplishment of the following: (1) The design and establishment of a regional network for monitoring shallow groundwater systems in the basin; (2) monitoring the direction and rate of flow, water quality, and aquifer characteristics of the shallow groundwater systems; and (3) development of a regional groundwater simulation model, with appurtenant subroutines to determine local effects.

entry.dc:title: MINING SHOVELS AND DRAGLINES REVIEWED.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: The major share of the market for machines to load or shift overburden and mineral at surface mining operations is held by rope operated shovels and draglines. This article outlines some of the trends in operational methods and reviews the ranges of equipment offered by the major manufacturers. Recently introduced machines are especially highlighted. The trend to modular designs to facilitate transportation, erection and maintenance is noted. The differing attributes of crawler and walking draglines are considered.

entry.dc:title: GET THE BIG PICTURE - TO COMPLY WITH RECLAMATION LAWS.
entry.dc:creator: Brumbaugh F.
entry.dc:description: The Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 has created a need for better reclamation technology and management. These needs can be met with remote sensing and normal field reconnaissance. By combining these methods, opeators can measure reclamation effectiveness and obtain reliable data for planning. The author emphasizes that remote sensing should be an integral part of a reclamation program. A complete reclamation management program should consist of conventional field reconnaissance; high and low altitude aerial photography; and selected satellite imagery.

entry.dc:title: SURFACE MINING REGULATIONS AND LITIGATION FOR 1978.
entry.dc:creator: Todd D.
entry.dc:description: This article covers the regulatory and litigation activities during 1978 regarding the Surface Mine Control and Reclamation Act and the regulations issued thereunder.

entry.dc:title: Ground‐Water Quality Standards — Irrelevant
entry.dc:creator: Rayner F.
entry.dc:description: Proposals to establish national ground‐water quality standards appear to be premature, and redundant because of the geohydrologic and geochemical factors governing the occurrence and development of ground water. Although it can be reasoned that there is no “good time” to establish additional governmental standards (and the resultant additional governmental regulations), it can also be strongly argued that now is a “bad time” to consider establishment of the proposed standards. First, a present mood of the general public is away from more governmental involvement in the business and private sectors, and a rebellion against the increasing cost of government. Second, the applicability and workability of present Federal (and some State) laws that could be used to adequately protect ground‐water quality, have yet to be implemented or otherwise sufficiently tested. The full force and effect of the Water Pollution Control Act (PL 92‐500 with amendments) has yet to be implemented, and Congress is still considering its “oversights” in their drafting of same. The Safe Drinking Water Act (PL 93‐523), particularly those sections designed or usable to protect ground‐water quality, have yet to be tested by the EPA. Like PL 92‐500, the deadline for implementation of parts of PL 93‐523 has long since passed. And the far‐reaching effects on ground‐water quality protection that three other federal laws‐the Resource Conservation Recovery Act (PL 94‐580); the Toxic Substances Control Act (PL 94‐469); and Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act (PL 95‐87)—are totally unknown, since the procedures for full implementation of these acts have yet to be developed. Therefore, it appears that establishing a new ground‐water quality control act prior to testing existing law and thereby learning from their flaws or shortcomings, could result in unnecessary proliferation of law without its reasonable testing. This appears to be good time to interrupt the geometric progression that tends to spawn additional laws when laws are developed ahead of their established need. Equitable and workable ground‐water quality protection could be fostered through the enactment of the long overdue requirements for the integration of surface‐and ground‐water development and management structures. This integration would decrease inefficiency of use of these water resources—which are actually inseparable in identity to their users, the American taxpayers. Copyright © 1979, Wiley Blackwell. entry.dc:title: Impact of human influences on the vegetation of the Western Himalaya
entry.dc:creator: Gupta R.
entry.dc:description: Effects of human influences on the vegetation of the Western Himalaya have been reviewed. Impacts of forest management practices, over-grazing, surface mining, defence and development operations, and road building activities, are severe in the region. This has created an alarming situation for soil and water conservation. Increased soil loss and runoff pose a threat to various reservoirs built for various uses and have increased hazards of erosion and floods in the Indus and Ganga basin regions. © 1978 Dr. W. Junk b.v. Publishers.

entry.dc:title: STABILITY OF SPOIL BANKS AND HOLLOW FILLS CREATED BY SURFACE MINING.
entry.dc:creator: Huang Y.H.
entry.prism:publicationName: Univ Ky Inst Min Miner Res Rep IMMR
entry.dc:description: This report describes work accomplished under a research project entitled ″Slope Stability of Spoil Banks from Surface Mining″ . A spoil bank is a sidehill bench formed by depositing the overburden materials removed from above a coal seam. The objectives of this research were twofold: first, to study the failure of spoil banks in Eastern Kentucky, so as to ascertain the causes of failure and the necessary preventive measures; and, secondly, to develop a practical method for determining the most appropriate slopes to be used for spoil banks under various conditions.

entry.dc:title: POLICY ALTERNATIVES FOR RECLAIMING SURFACE MINED LANDS.
entry.dc:creator: Greenbaum M.
entry.prism:publicationName: Univ Ky Inst Min Miner Res Rep IMMR
entry.dc:description: Recently enacted surface mining controls express congressional concern with the potential for environmental damage. But how to implement the new statutes while preserving congressional intent remains a controversial issue. Resolution is left largely to federal agencies and the affected states. This paper addresses the issue of how best to internalize the external costs created by surface coal mining. Section II is an examination of the inherent difficulties of operationalizing a Pigouvian solution. Section III is a review of an example of actual regulation and policy based on the case of Eastern Kentucky; and Section IV offers suggestions as to the advantages and disadvantages of alternative policy tools.

entry.dc:title: Land use and national coal surface mining policies.
entry.dc:creator: Anderson M.
entry.dc:description: The prime cropland provisions of Public Law 95-87 are the only ones which can potentially cause major disturbances in production, and then only in the Midwest, particularly in Illinois. Even in Illinois, the known reserves under unprotected lands are several hundred times greater than current yearly production. While thousands of acres will be reclaimed under the Abandoned Mine Fund provisions, this must be viewed as a very long term program to address the damages of over a century of virtually unregulated mining. Future development plans of mine operators will have to be compatible with land use regulations, or delayed mine openings or expansions could adversely affect production.- from U.S.Govt. Reports Announcements, 4, 1980

entry.dc:title: Surface mining and fish/ wildlife needs in the eastern United States. Proc. symposium held at Morgantown, West Virginia, 3-6 Dec. 1978.
entry.dc:creator: Samuel D.E.
entry.dc:description: The report describes a state-of-the-art overview on surface mining in the eastern US and the fish/wildlife relationships; best methods for measuring mining impacts; the effects of mining on the biota; mined land reclamation techniques for fish/wildlife benefits; and opportunities for improving fish/wildlife habitat on mined lands. Information is provided by the mining industry, conservation groups, and state and federal agencies. -from US Govt Reports Announcements, 23, 1979

entry.dc:title: IMPACT OF COAL UTILIZATION IN TEXAS UNDER THE NATIONAL ENERGY PLAN.
entry.dc:creator: Kaiser W.R.
entry.dc:description: The authors discuss that the National Energy Plant goal is to double coal consumption by 1985 where the intent is to completely phase out natural gas as a boiler fuel by 1990. At the same time coal consumption is to be doubled while environmental quality is to be maintained by implementing the stringent 1977 Clean Air Act Amendments and the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977.
